clue.text: Wrongfully convict us-jury's conclusion is rank

indicators.note: something done wrongfully is done amiss, so the letters of the two words are set out in a new order
the conclusion of a word is its final letter, here taken from the word jury's

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a jury has wrongly convicted them, and the verdict is outrageous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rank' looks like an adjective (outrageous) closing the protest, but it is the noun: a title of nobility. 'Wrongfully' rearranges CONVICTUS, and 'conclusion' adds the Y ending 'jury's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A viscountcy is the title and status of a viscount, a grade in the peerage.

clue.text: Box in, to be on the safe side

definitions.meaning: to enclose in a box or container, a variant spelling of encase

definitions.text: to be on the safe side
definitions.meaning: as a precaution, for safety

explanation.surface: Packing things into a box as a precaution.
explanation.walkthrough: The run-together form is an old variant of encase; split into two words it is the phrase for a precaution.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to enclose in a container, and split in two the phrase means as a precaution.

clue.text: Bishop's position helps give Capablanca the draw

indicators.note: these words help supply the letters, as part of the run across Capablanca the draw spells out the entry

explanation.surface: A chess bishop's placement helps Capablanca secure a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: Capablanca was a Cuban world chess champion, so 'Bishop' looks like a chess piece. The letters run from the end of 'Capablanca' through 'the' into 'draw'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedra is the bishop's throne in his cathedral, the seat of his authority, as in ex cathedra.

clue.text: Everywhere at once, like the monarch in court

definitions.meaning: present in all places at the same time
English legal theory holds that the sovereign is present in every court of law at once

explanation.surface: The king seems to turn up everywhere at court.
explanation.walkthrough: In English law the Crown is deemed present in all its courts, a legal fiction called the king's ubiquity.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means omnipresent, and legal theory treats the sovereign as present in every court.

clue.text: Holds how much in them?

parts.note: holds are the cargo spaces of a ship, and the question asks the measure of what can be carried in them

explanation.surface: A question about how much someone is holding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: the cargo spaces below a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's capacity for cargo is measured in tons, the figure for how much its holds carry.

clue.text: Way up north this is a bore

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Somewhere far up in the north, this place is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the way upside down, as befits a down clue. 'Way up north' reads as a remote place, but it is all mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious is a bore, and also something that makes you open your mouth from tiredness.

clue.text: Fall the usual way-or up, remarkably

parts.note: things normally fall towards the ground, so the usual direction is downward

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something strange has happened, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Things usually fall downwards, but remarkably they might go up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkably' rearranges 'or up'. 'Fall' looks like a tumble, but it is a fall of rain; the usual way anything falls is towards the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy fall of rain is a deluge.

clue.text: Valuation of property item takes in Nazis:

indicators.note: one word takes in the other, holding it inside

parts.note: an asset is a single item of property
SS men were members of the Nazi Schutzstaffel

explanation.surface: A valuation of a property item reveals it harbours Nazis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' puts SS MEN inside ASSET.
explanation.definitionFit: A valuation is an appraisal of worth, as in a tax appraisal of a property.

clue.text: Alias for T. E. Lawrence (see above)

definitions.meaning: Lawrence of Arabia enlisted in the RAF as Aircraftman Ross
on the printed page the heading over this list of clues is the direction word for these clues

explanation.surface: A trivia note about Lawrence of Arabia's assumed name, with a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: After the war Lawrence hid in the ranks as Aircraftman Ross. The second definition is a joke about the page: look above this clue and the heading names the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's RAF pseudonym was Aircraftman Ross, and the heading printed above the clue lists the horizontal entries.

clue.text: Coming from Black Sea area in yachts, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words are only one possible arrangement of the letters, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone arriving by yacht from the Black Sea region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IN YACHTS. Scythia was the ancient land north of the Black Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Scythians lived on the steppes north of the Black Sea, so the adjective describes people from that region.

clue.text: The sort of fudge Lear produced

definitions.text: The sort of fudge Lear produced

parts.words: The sort of fudge Lear produced
parts.note: fudge here means rubbish or humbug rather than a sweet, and Edward Lear was the Victorian author of absurd comic verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat

explanation.surface: A confectioner called Lear and the kind of fudge he made.
explanation.walkthrough: Fudge suggests sweets, and Lear the king, but Edward Lear wrote celebrated books of comic verse in a genre named for silly talk, and fudge is an old word for such silly talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear's Book of Nonsense made his name, and fudge as an exclamation means rubbish or humbug.

clue.text: Study — just added to make change again

definitions.meaning: to study is to pore over a text

definitions.text: just added to make change again
definitions.meaning: add the word just to the end of this entry and the result is a verb meaning adjust once more

explanation.surface: A note that study, with something just added, leads to a change of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a word-building riddle: put JUST after the answer and you get a verb meaning to change again (re-adjust).
explanation.definitionFit: To study a book is to peruse it; with the word just tacked on, it becomes the verb for altering a setting once more.

clue.text: Meeting-place the French provided for us

definitions.text: Meeting-place the French provided for us

parts.words: Meeting-place the French provided for us
parts.note: a spot for a meeting, named by a word English borrowed from French

explanation.surface: A meeting spot set up for us by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: The French gave English this word, literally 'present yourselves', as their gift of a meeting-place.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendezvous is an arranged place to meet, a loanword from French.

clue.text: Shameful, unlike Howe's victory day

parts.note: a negating prefix that makes a word mean the opposite, as in inactive
Admiral Howe's naval victory over the French in 1794 is known as the Glorious First of June

explanation.surface: A dishonourable act, nothing like Admiral Howe's day of triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: The Glorious First of June (1794) was Admiral Howe's victory over the French fleet; 'unlike' it means not glorious.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without glory brings disgrace, so it is dishonourable or shameful.

clue.text: Economist in novel, missing nothing, taking in everything

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of the two words take a new arrangement
missing means the letters lack something, so a letter for nothing is left out of the mix

parts.note: O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An economist in a novel who misses nothing and takes everything in.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ECONOMISTIN, lose the O ('nothing', removed by 'missing'), and rearrange ('novel') the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: All-knowing: one who grasps and understands everything.

clue.text: Horse not supporting a figure? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: the pieces go in the opposite order to the clue's, so the word for not comes before the horse

parts.note: no is used for not, as in no good
a nag is an old or poor horse
on, as in a thing resting on another and supported by it

explanation.surface: A horse that does not hold up a statue, or the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, 'Horse not supporting' gives the pieces in the wrong order; 'Quite the opposite' puts the negative word before the horse. 'a figure' is a geometric shape, not a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: A nine-sided polygon is a geometric figure.

clue.text: Bede's sound constituents of this ornament

definitions.text: Bede's sound constituents of this ornament

parts.words: Bede's sound constituents of this ornament
parts.note: the Venerable Bede's name with an s sounds like the small pierced balls threaded together to make a piece of jewellery

explanation.surface: The sound parts of the Venerable Bede's ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: The Venerable Bede was an Anglo-Saxon monk and historian; 'Bede's' said aloud is 'beads', which make up this ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: A string of beads is worn round the neck as jewellery.

clue.text: Send Morse, wanting leaders to confirm decision

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, and the leaders are the opening letters of both words, so each word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to send a Morse message to confirm a ruling.
explanation.walkthrough: SEND and MORSE each lose their first letter, leaving END + ORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse a decision is to approve or ratify it, giving it your backing.

clue.text: Work in theatre for top rate, perhaps, round 21

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round, enclosing the other piece
perhaps hints the letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are reordered

parts.note: 21 across is the compass point, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: A theatre production for which actors are paid the top rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TOP RATE, and 'round' wraps those letters about E, the abbreviation of the answer to 21 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A short, light comic opera is a work staged in a theatre.

clue.text: Right principles for Irish bog-trotters, originally

definitions.meaning: the doctrine of the political right, conservatism
the party name first meant a dispossessed Irish outlaw, a Gaelic term for a pursued man

explanation.surface: Correct principles that Irish bog-dwellers originally lived by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory' comes from Irish tóraidhe, a hunted outlaw, used in the 17th century for Irish bandits ('bog-trotters', an old slur on the Irish) before it named the British Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The creed of the British Conservative party, whose nickname first meant an Irish outlaw.

clue.text: Pleasure trips sometimes preceded by alarms

definitions.meaning: outings or jaunts taken for enjoyment
the Elizabethan stage direction alarums and ..., meaning noisy battle scenes

explanation.surface: Holidays that are sometimes preceded by worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alarums and excursions' is an old stage direction for battle noise and troop movements, now a phrase for commotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Outings for enjoyment are jaunts; the phrase alarums and excursions puts the word after alarms.

clue.text: Direction of career in writing by Disraeli

definitions.meaning: a compass point
in Disraeli's novel Tancred a character declares that the Orient is a career

explanation.surface: Disraeli's career in writing took a certain direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli's novel Tancred (1847) contains the line 'The East is a career'. 'of' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the four compass points, and the region Disraeli's Tancred called a career.

clue.text: It's still an atmospheric disturbance

definitions.meaning: motionless, not moving
crackling interference on a radio, caused by electrical charge in the air

explanation.surface: It is still a disturbance in the atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'still' looks like an adverb (even now), but it is the adjective: unmoving. 'It's' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means unmoving, and the noun names crackle on the radio from charges in the air.

clue.text: Evil — in vain, by end of play

definitions.text: Evil — in vain, by end of play

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other, the wickedness sitting within the word for futile

parts.note: taken as written
ill means evil or harm, as in speak ill of

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here taken from play

explanation.surface: Wickedness proves futile when the play ends, as villains always get their comeuppance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the word for evil inside 'vain', and 'end of' adds the last letter of 'play'. Taken whole, the clue is the stage scoundrel's wickedness defeated by the final act.
explanation.definitionFit: Wickedness or vile conduct, the behaviour of a stage scoundrel, which melodramas show coming to nothing at the final curtain.

clue.text: Sounds as if I possess a Hebridean island

indicators.note: the words are spoken, and what is heard gives the entry

parts.note: to possess is to own, so this phrase becomes I own a

explanation.surface: A claim to own one of the Hebridean islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I own a' said aloud gives the island's name. The Hebrides are islands off Scotland's west coast; this one holds St Columba's abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small island of the Inner Hebrides off Mull, famed for St Columba's monastery.

clue.text: Personality obvious in some twins

definitions.meaning: a person's individual character, who they are
sameness, plainly seen in twins who look alike

explanation.surface: A personality trait that shows up clearly in some twins.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is sameness: identical twins show it obviously.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both one's individual self and exact likeness, as seen in identical twins.

clue.text: Young ragamuffin, a feature of the old city

indicators.note: the facial feature belongs to and follows the city, so the city name comes first

parts.note: Ur is the ancient city of Mesopotamia, a crossword favourite
the chin is a feature of the face

explanation.surface: A scruffy child who is a familiar sight in the old part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: Feature means a part of the face, not a landmark. 'of' puts the ancient Sumerian city first.
explanation.definitionFit: A street urchin is a poor, scruffy child, a ragamuffin.

clue.text: Once an acknowledgment to remedy an outsider's deficiency

definitions.meaning: in older usage the word meant an admission or concession of something
what someone outside lacks is entry, and being let in supplies it

explanation.surface: An archaic note that an apology once made up for a stranger's shortcomings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an obsolete sense: an admission or acknowledgment. The second sense is entry, which is what someone shut outside lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: The word formerly meant an admission or concession, and now means permission to enter, which cures an outsider's lack of access.
